description:
🚀 We are a passionate team participating in NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026, exploring the stories and legacy of forgotten space missions. We are interested in programming, web development, research, and creative problem-solving.

We welcome motivated teammates with skills in web development, UI/UX design, data analysis, astronomy, or storytelling. Beginners are welcome too!

Let's bring forgotten space stories back to life! 🌌
summary:
**High-Level Project Summary**

NASA Archive is an interactive 3D website that helps people discover the machines humans have left on the Moon, on Mars and in deep space. Visitors rotate a 3D scene, click a spacecraft, and ask questions in English or Arabic. An AI storyteller answers with a short, kid-friendly story about that machine: why it was sent, how it worked, what it discovered, and where it is today. We built it for the challenge "Abandoned but not Forgotten".

The site covers 13 groups of NASA hardware, from the Apollo Lunar Modules and Surveyor landers to Sojourner, Viking, Ingenuity, Dawn, Pioneer and Kepler. Each group has its own storyteller, which answers from a knowledge base built from official NASA data. If a fact is missing, it can search trusted sources such as NASA, JPL, ESA, universities and museums. If it still cannot find the answer, it says so instead of guessing.

This matters because many of these explorers finished their missions long ago, and their data is hard for students and curious readers to approach. NASA Archive turns that data into stories that are simple, accurate and easy to enjoy, so these machines stay remembered and more people, including Arabic-speaking learners, feel connected to the science they made possible.
details:
Project Details

What it does

NASA Archive is an interactive 3D website for exploring the machines humans left on the Moon, on Mars and in deep space. The Explore page shows these places as a 3D scene with spacecraft orbiting them. Visitors drag to rotate the scene, choose Moon, Mars or Deep Space, and click a spacecraft. A chat then lets them ask questions about that machine in English or Arabic. An AI storyteller replies with a short, kid-friendly story built from official NASA data.

The main use is learning: a student or curious reader can understand a mission in about two minutes, without reading technical documents. The target audience is school-age space fans (about 10 to 16) and casual readers.

How it works

  1. The visitor picks a machine. The website sends the question and that machine’s ID to our backend.
  2. The backend is an n8n workflow behind a secured webhook (header authentication). It routes the request by ID to one of 13 storyteller configurations, each with its own scope.
  3. The storyteller is an AI agent. Before answering, it searches a knowledge base of NASA facts about that machine only. This keeps answers grounded in sources and stops facts from one mission leaking into another.
  4. If the knowledge base lacks a fact, or the question is about the machine’s current status, the agent can run a web search and trust only NASA, JPL, ESA, universities and museums.
  5. The answer returns to the chat as plain text, in the visitor’s language.

How the data supports it

We collected official NASA information on each machine and split it into short text chunks. Each chunk is embedded separately and stored in a vector database with the ID of its machine. When a question arrives, the agent retrieves the most relevant chunks for that machine and tells the story from them. The storytelling is written in our own words, not copied from the source text. The agent must state every name, number and date exactly as sourced. If a source says “unknown”, “assumed” or “estimated”, the answer says the same, and if no source has the answer, it says so instead of guessing.

Hardware covered (13 storytellers)

Moon: Apollo Lunar Modules, Apollo Lunar Roving Vehicles, ALSEP and EASEP science packages, Surveyor landers.
Mars: Mars Pathfinder and Sojourner, Spirit and Opportunity, Viking 1 and 2, InSight, Ingenuity.
Deep space: Dawn, NEAR Shoemaker, Pioneer 10 and 11, Kepler and K2.

Storytelling and safety design

Each answer follows the machine’s journey: why it was sent, how it worked, what it discovered, and its status today. The engineering is linked to the science, so the reader sees why the machine’s design led to a specific discovery. The AI stays a narrator and never speaks as the machine. Replies are short, use simple words and a few meaningful emojis, and keep mission and equipment names in English even inside Arabic text. Content stays suitable for children, and off-topic questions are politely declined.

Benefits and what we hope to achieve

Many of these explorers finished their work long ago, and their data is hard for non-specialists to approach. We hope to keep their stories alive, make space history easier to learn, and widen access for Arabic-speaking learners.

Tools and technologies

  • Frontend: interactive 3D web app, hosted on GitHub Pages
  • Backend and automation: n8n (webhook, routing, AI agent)
  • Knowledge base: Supabase vector store
  • Embeddings: Google Gemini embeddings
  • Language model: accessed through OpenRouter
  • Backup web search: SerpApi
  • Data: official NASA mission data

Working features (delivered)

  • Interactive 3D explorer with Moon (4), Mars (5) and Deep Space (4) groups
  • 13 separate storytellers routed by machine ID
  • Chat in English and Arabic
  • Retrieval from a per-machine knowledge base, with a trusted-source web search as backup
  • Secured backend endpoint

Limitations

  • Answers are only as complete as our knowledge base. Some machines have detailed data and others have shorter summaries, so deep questions on lesser-covered machines may get shorter answers.
  • Current-status facts can change over time, and they depend on the web search backup when our data does not cover them.
  • All visitors currently share one chat memory.

Future plans (not yet built)

  • Separate chat memory for each visitor
  • More spacecraft, added by giving each one new data chunks, a routing rule and a scope description
  • Voice narration and more languages
  • Short sourced timelines for each machine
